title: The Zafarnama's opening
hook: the letter to Aurangzeb begins with praise of God in Persian verse (Zafarnama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a son's lines for his father: he gave his head, but not his faith. Your line was head, not faith.

The draft sits on the screen. It's to someone who wronged you badly, someone with power. The first line you typed is all heat: how could you. Plenty of people have written that first line and deleted it at two in the morning. Guru Gobind Singh wrote a letter like this to the emperor Aurangzeb. He wrote it in Persian, the language of the emperor's court, in verse. And the first thing he put on the page wasn't the emperor at all.
screen: `THE LETTER TO SOMEONE WITH POWER.` → `ALL HEAT IN THE FIRST LINE.` → `THE GURU'S LETTER BEGINS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: The letter is the Zafarnama, which you met on day ninety-two. Tradition says it was carried to the emperor by a Sikh messenger, and that it was written in a season of great loss. Its hard words come tomorrow. Today, only its opening, and the opening is praise. In paraphrase, the first lines call on God as perfect in wonders, eternal and generous, the giver of contentment, the provider, the deliverer, the merciful. The Lord who gives without being asked, who holds the earth and the sky, who keeps the whole world fed. Line after line, the names keep coming before a single word goes to the man the letter is for. Notice the language. Persian, and names for God like the Merciful, the Provider, the Generous: names the emperor's own faith also uses. It's the move Akal Ustat made a few days ago: different names, one Lord. The Guru begins the letter on ground the two men share. And the praise frames everything after it. Before any complaint, the letter sets the scene: there is a Judge above both of us, and you and I stand in front of Him. Whatever comes next, a rebuke, a reminder, a demand for honesty, it comes inside that frame. That's not flattery of God to soften the blow. It sets the whole quarrel under Someone greater than either man. Whatever he'd been through, the Guru's first act on the page was to praise. The anger is real, and it's coming. But it doesn't get the first word.
screen: `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.` · `IT OPENS WITH THE NAMES OF GOD.` · `SHARED NAMES, SHARED GROUND.` · `A JUDGE ABOVE BOTH OF THEM.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one message you need to send: an email you've been dreading, a text to someone you're at odds with. Before thinking about what you need to say, find something true and good you both stand on, and let that be the first line, inwardly; the rest can wait. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath out.
The Zafarnama's opening. The tenth Guru's Persian letter to the emperor begins not with the emperor, but with the names of God: the Generous, the Provider, the Merciful. Today's word.
Your line: begin with praise. One Judge stands above both the writer and the reader. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Zafarnama is included in the Dasam Granth; Sikhs read and recite it in its original Persian and in translation, and its opening is read as praise of God.

chat.says: Why would the Guru open an angry letter to the emperor with praise?
options: The praise is for God, not the emperor: it sets their quarrel under a Judge above both.
To flatter the emperor first, so he'd be in a good mood to read the rest.
Because the letter was really a prayer, and it was never meant to be sent.
chat.meaning: Before a word goes to the emperor, the Zafarnama praises God, the Generous, the Provider, the Merciful, setting the whole quarrel under Someone greater.

notes: The opening couplets are paraphrased from memory; please check the list of divine names (perfect in wonders, eternal, generous, giver of contentment, provider, deliverer, merciful) and the 'earth and sky' and 'keeps the world fed' lines.
The messenger is left unnamed and framed as tradition (often given as Bhai Daya Singh); the 'season of great loss' is also framed as tradition, with no events named. Please confirm.
The claim that these names would be familiar from the emperor's own prayers is an interpretive note; please confirm it is fair and respectful to Muslims.
The title is commonly rendered 'epistle of victory'; that gloss was left out under the claims rule. A Keeper may add it.
Original game uses Persian script (the letter's language) rather than Gurmukhi; please check spelling, or swap for ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ.
